# Why Model It First? {.unnumbered}

A fence, a deck, and a shed are forgiving projects until they are not. A post
set 50 mm out of line, a joist that misses its footing, or a gate that swings
into a downspout can turn a weekend into a second trip to the lumber yard. CAD
is a rehearsal: you build the thing once on screen, find the collisions and
awkward dimensions, and then build it for real with a cut list in hand.

This book is a hands-on introduction to [SolidCraft](https://solidcraft.app)
and [FreeCAD](https://www.freecad.org) for carpentry and exterior construction.
It assumes you know, or want to learn, how a fence, deck, or shed goes
together. It does not assume any CAD experience.

::: {.callout-note}
## This book is a working skeleton

The chapter files contain outlines and learning goals rather than finished
prose, with `TODO` markers where figures and exact commands still need to be
added. Work through a track in order. As you learn a technique, replace the
outline with your own explanation, screenshots, and a tested model. The
structure is deliberately stable so the material can grow without being
reorganized every time.
:::

## What you will build

- **A fence panel and gate:** posts, rails, pickets, a braced gate frame, and
  the clearances that keep a gate swinging.
- **A small deck:** posts, beams, joists, decking, guard, and stairs, modeled
  as a set of repeated parts.
- **A gable shed:** a floor platform, stud walls, openings, and a simple roof,
  with enough detail to produce a cut list.

You build each project twice: once in SolidCraft (Parts I–III) and once in
FreeCAD (Part IV). The FreeCAD shed also adds a BIM model and IFC export.

## How to use this book

Start with the historical and practical overview in the Introduction. Then pick
a track:

- **SolidCraft track:** Parts I–III. It builds the mental model, the
  carpentry-specific habits, and the three projects.
- **FreeCAD track:** Part IV. It teaches Sketcher, Part Design, Spreadsheets,
  TechDraw, BIM/IFC, and the same three projects.
- **Full course:** read both. The concepts transfer; the workflows differ enough
  to be worth comparing.

Part I is useful before either track because it covers units, datums, sketches,
and parameters. Part II adds components, joinery, clearances, takeoffs, and the
OpenCode workflow. Part III applies them in SolidCraft. Part IV does the same
work in FreeCAD and ends with a chapter on choosing and combining the tools.

Most chapters follow the same shape:

- **What you will learn** — the small number of ideas to take away.
- **Build along** — one model to make while reading.
- **Checks** — the measurements that tell you the model is right.
- **Exercises** — variations worth trying before moving on.

You can follow in each tool's interface or drive it with an AI assistant
connected through OpenCode. The concepts are the same; the commands, menus, and
workbench names differ.

## Conventions used in this book

- **Units are millimetres.** Wood dimensions, hardware, and site measurements
  are all easier to keep consistent in one unit. Both tools can display other
  units, but the models here use mm.
- **Z is up.** The XY plane is the plan view, XZ and YZ are elevations. Ground
  level is normally Z = 0 unless a chapter says otherwise.
- **Model actual dimensions.** A "2 × 4" is not 50 × 100 mm. Model the wood you
  can actually buy, and write down the nominal name separately.
- **Pick a datum and keep it.** Put the origin at a sensible corner, face, or
  ground line, and document it. Most mysterious dimension errors are datum
  errors.
- **Model the fit, not the grain.** CAD is good at clearance, spacing, and
  collisions. It cannot tell you whether a board will cup or a knot will weaken
  a joint.

## A safety note

::: {.callout-warning}
This book teaches modeling, not structural engineering. Spans, footing sizes,
guard heights, wind uplift, snow loads, permits, and attachment details are
governed by local building codes and site conditions. Have a qualified person
review anything structural, and follow the hardware manufacturer's instructions.
No model in this book replaces that review.
:::

## The book at a glance

| Part | Chapters | Outcome |
|------|----------|---------|
| Introduction | — | Where CAD came from and why tool choice matters |
| Foundations | 1–5 | Sketch, extrude, and parameterize a simple part in SolidCraft |
| SolidCraft modeling | 6–10 | Repeat parts, model joinery, check fit, produce figures and a BOM, and drive SolidCraft with OpenCode |
| SolidCraft projects | 11–15 | Model a fence, a deck, a shed, and its site |
| FreeCAD | 16–24 | Part Design, spreadsheets, TechDraw, BIM/IFC, the same three projects, FreeCAD with OpenCode, and tool choice |
| Appendices | A–E | Command map, troubleshooting, glossary, open-source landscape, FreeCAD setup |

Ready? Start with the [Introduction](chapters/00-introduction.qmd), then go to
[A Tour of SolidCraft](chapters/01-solidcraft-tour.qmd) for the SolidCraft
track, or [FreeCAD for SolidCraft Users](chapters/16-freecad-tour.qmd) for the
FreeCAD track.
